findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: design.md#Context states: "Business customers often share a purchasing mailbox (`orders@acme.example`) between several buyers, each with their own customer record and billing address." The load-bearing assumption "an e-mail address identifies exactly one person" is refuted by the design's own Context: several buyers sharing `orders@acme.example` each have their own record and billing address. As written, the nightly job would collapse those distinct buyers into the oldest one, reassign all their orders to it and delete their records with their billing addresses — it builds the wrong thing for business customers. Choose a key that separates them (e.g. e-mail plus name and billing address, or restrict the merge to guest-created records with matching identity fields), or exclude shared mailboxes explicitly, and state that rule in the design and the spec. Add a spec scenario "Two buyers share a purchasing mailbox → both records remain" and test it in task 1.1.
findings.title: The merge key rests on an assumption the design's own context contradicts

findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The job deletes customer records (with their name and billing address) every night, and the plan gives no backup, no record of which orders moved from which customer, no dry run and no staged rollout. A wrong merge — such as the shared-mailbox case of R-skeptic-1 — cannot be undone. Plan a way back: keep a merge log (old id → kept id, original row) or soft-delete the merged records, and start with a dry-run report before enabling deletion; add a task for it.
findings.title: Deleting merged customers is a one-way door with no way back

findings.evidence: A nightly job SHALL merge customer records that share an e-mail address into the oldest one, moving their orders to it.
findings.recommendation: The design groups by "lower-cased e-mail", but the requirement says only "share an e-mail address", and its two scenarios (`ada@example.org` twice, all distinct) cannot tell whether `Ada@Example.org` and `ada@example.org` must merge. There is no scenario for case or surrounding whitespace differences, for three or more records (which one is kept, ties on `created_at`), nor for a record that is not a duplicate of the same person. State the normalization in the requirement and add those scenarios, then name them in task 1.1.
findings.title: The spec covers only the happy path and does not pin down what "share an e-mail address" means

findings.recommendation: The proposal adds "A nightly job merges customers that share an e-mail address." — something that must be scheduled, monitored and run against production data — yet `operations` is unticked without a reason, so no expert reviews how it is run, alerted on or stopped. Tick it, or keep it unticked with the reason on its line.
findings.title: A new scheduled job is introduced with the operations domain unticked and no reason
